questions.q: What is the primary chemical process that causes concrete to harden?
o: Hydration (The chemical reaction between cement and water).
questions.n: Hydration is the exothermic chemical reaction where cement and water form a stony substance.

questions.q: True or False: Heat is the primary agent that hardens concrete.
o: False (Heat can actually cause premature drying and cracking; water is the key).
questions.n: Concrete hardens through a chemical reaction with water; excessive heat can steal that water and ruin the concrete.

questions.q: What is the standard concrete cover for footings cast against and permanently exposed to earth?
questions.n: The NSCP mandates 75mm of cover when concrete is cast directly against soil to protect the steel from moisture and minerals.

questions.q: What is the standard concrete cover for columns and beams not exposed to weather or earth?
questions.n: For interior structural members like columns and beams, 40mm is the standard protective distance to the main reinforcement.

questions.q: What is another term for a 'Pad Footing' that supports a single column?
questions.n: An isolated footing is designed to carry the load of a single column to the ground.

questions.q: What is the best paint texture for an exterior masonry wall to balance durability and aesthetic?
o: Semi-gloss (It offers better moisture resistance than flat and hides more imperfections than high-gloss).
questions.n: Semi-gloss provides the ideal middle ground for outdoor protection and visual smoothness.

questions.q: Which paint type is highly recommended for exterior concrete due to its ability to bridge hairline cracks?
questions.n: Elastomeric paints are thick and flexible, allowing them to stretch and cover minor concrete cracks.

questions.q: In concrete terminology, what do you call the process of maintaining moisture and temperature to ensure proper hydration?
questions.n: Curing is the vital period after placement where moisture is preserved to allow maximum strength gain.

questions.q: Which material is commonly used as a "water stop" in construction joints of concrete tanks?
questions.n: These materials are embedded in the concrete to block the passage of liquid through joints.

questions.q: Why is "honeycombing" in concrete a structural concern?
o: It makes the concrete surface look rough.
It suggests the concrete was over-hydrated.
It indicates voids where the coarse aggregate was not properly surrounded by mortar, reducing strength and exposing rebar.
It increases the weight of the concrete.
questions.n: Voids weaken the structural integrity and allow corrosive elements to reach the reinforcement.

questions.q: What is the purpose of adding "Retarders" to a concrete mix?
o: To speed up the hardening process.
To slow down the initial setting time, usually in hot weather or for large pours.
questions.n: This prevents 'cold joints' and gives workers more time to finish the concrete.

questions.q: What is a "Slump Test" used for?
o: To measure the consistency and workability of fresh concrete.
To test the air content of the mix.
To check the moisture content of the soil.
To determine the final compressive strength.
questions.n: It determines if the mix is too wet, too dry, or just right for the project requirements.

questions.q: Which cement type is considered "High Early Strength"?
questions.n: Type III is ground finer to react faster, reaching 7-day strength in about 3 days.

questions.q: What happens to concrete if the "Water-Cement Ratio" is too high?
o: The concrete becomes easier to cure.
It improves the bond with the rebar.
The concrete becomes more porous and its ultimate strength is significantly reduced.
questions.n: Excess water leaves behind microscopic voids (capillaries) when it evaporates, weakening the structure.

questions.q: What do you call the horizontal reinforcement used in CHB (Concrete Hollow Block) walls?
questions.n: These bars are laid in the grooves of the blocks to provide lateral stability.

questions.q: What is the structural enclosure (shaft) that supports and contains the elevator car?
questions.n: The hoistway is the vertical space or shaft in which the elevator car travels.

questions.q: What is the main compartment where passengers or goods are carried in an elevator?
questions.n: The cabin is the enclosed platform designed to carry the occupant load.

questions.q: What do you call the heavy weights used to balance the load of the elevator car?
questions.n: Counterweights offset the weight of the car plus about 40-50% of the rated capacity to save energy.

questions.q: Which component acts as a safety device to stop the elevator car if it exceeds its rated speed?
questions.n: The governor monitors speed and triggers the safety brakes if the car falls or speeds out of control.

questions.q: What is the name of the pulley with grooves that the hoisting cables run through?
questions.n: A sheave is a specialized pulley that uses friction to move the cables.

questions.q: What is the name of the buffer located at the bottom of the hoistway to soften the impact of the car or counterweight?
questions.n: The buffer is a spring or oil-filled cylinder designed to stop a descending car in an emergency.

questions.q: Which type of elevator is primarily used for low-rise buildings and uses a piston to move the car?
questions.n: Hydraulic systems use fluid pressure to push a plunger/piston, limited by the depth of the cylinder.

questions.q: Which type of elevator is used for high-rise buildings and uses cables and sheaves?
questions.n: Traction elevators use cables and counterweights, making them efficient for great heights.

questions.q: Name a globally recognized brand of elevators.
questions.n: These companies are the world leaders in vertical transportation systems.

questions.q: What do you call the horizontal, revolving stairs used to transport people between floors?
questions.n: Escalators are power-driven, inclined, continuous stairs.

questions.q: What is the standard angle of inclination for an escalator?
questions.n: This is the international standard to balance safety, space, and comfort.

questions.q: What is the "Comb Plate" on an escalator?
o: The section at the top and bottom where the moving steps meet the stationary floor.
The panel that hides the motor.
questions.n: It has teeth (like a comb) that fit into the grooves of the steps to prevent objects from being caught.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the "Governor Switch"?
o: To change the direction of the elevator.
To cut off power to the motor before the mechanical safety brakes are applied.
questions.n: It acts as the first line of defense during an overspeed event.

questions.q: In an elevator, what is a "Traveling Cable"?
o: The cable that connects the counterweight.
The wire that pulls the car up.
The flexible cable that provides electrical connection between the moving car and the controller.
questions.n: It hangs in a loop and carries power and signals to the car as it moves.

questions.q: What is a "Dumbwaiter"?
o: A specialized service elevator for janitors.
An elevator with no sound system.
A manual pulley system for laundry.
A small freight elevator intended to carry objects rather than people.
questions.n: Commonly used in restaurants or hospitals to move food or supplies between floors.

questions.q: Which part of a generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy?
questions.n: The alternator uses electromagnetic induction to produce AC power.

questions.q: Which part of the generator provides the mechanical energy (the "prime mover")?
questions.n: The internal combustion engine is the source of rotational force for the alternator.

questions.q: What component in a generator ensures that the output voltage remains constant?
questions.n: The AVR adjusts the exciter current to maintain a stable voltage output.

questions.q: What is the typical wattage of a standard kitchen blender?
questions.n: Standard household blenders operate within this range for common mixing tasks.

questions.q: What is the purpose of an Automatic Transfer Switch (ATS)?
o: To measure how much fuel the generator has used.
To increase the voltage of the generator.
To protect the generator from lightning.
To automatically switch the power source from the main utility to the generator during a power failure.
questions.n: It safely disconnects the utility and connects the backup power to prevent back-feeding.

questions.q: What electrical device is used to store energy and provide a smooth current to electronic devices?
questions.n: It contains batteries and circuitry to bridge power gaps and filter spikes.

questions.q: Which part of the generator manages the fuel and air mixture?
o: Carburetor (for gas) or Fuel Injector (for diesel).
questions.n: These components ensure the correct ratio of fuel and air for combustion.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the "Stator" in an alternator?
o: It is the part that rotates to create the magnetic field.
It is the stationary part that contains the windings where electricity is induced.
questions.n: As the rotor turns, the stator's stationary coils capture the flowing current.

questions.q: In a hotel room, what device often requires a key card to activate the room's power?
questions.n: It ensures lights and AC are off when guests leave the room.

questions.q: What is the function of a "Timer Switch" in building utilities?
o: To count the number of residents.
To act as a main circuit breaker.
To automatically turn lights or equipment on/off at specific times to save energy.
To measure the speed of the motor.
questions.n: Commonly used for outdoor security lights or water pumps.

questions.q: What do you call the total power consumption of all connected devices in a circuit?
questions.n: It is the sum of the continuous ratings of all equipment connected to the supply system.

questions.q: What is the standard voltage for residential outlets in the Philippines?
questions.n: The Philippines follows this higher voltage standard for its national power grid.

questions.q: Which type of light fixture is often used for "Emergency Lights"?
questions.n: These have a built-in battery and two adjustable heads to illuminate exit paths during power failure.

questions.q: What do you call the protective device that "trips" or breaks the circuit during an overload?
questions.n: A circuit breaker is a switch designed to open automatically when it detects an overcurrent.

questions.q: What is the purpose of "Grounding" in an electrical system?
o: To boost the signal for the Wi-Fi.
To provide a safe path for fault current to return to the earth, preventing shocks.
questions.n: It ensures that metal enclosures don't become live and dangerous during a short circuit.

questions.q: Which valve uses a rotating ball with a hole to control the flow of water?
questions.n: A 90-degree turn opens or closes the spherical plug, providing a quick shut-off.

questions.q: Which valve is best for fully open or fully closed service and features a plate that slides up and down?
questions.n: A gate valve's wedge/disc moves vertically, making it ideal for isolation but poor for throttling.

questions.q: Which fitting is specifically designed to allow fluid to flow in only one direction?
questions.n: Check valves prevent backflow (back-siphonage) by allowing flow in only the desired direction.

questions.q: Which valve uses a "rotary" motion of the handle to move a plug into a seat to regulate flow?
questions.n: The design of a globe valve creates more resistance, making it the best choice for throttling or regulating flow.

questions.q: What type of pipe is commonly used for "Main" water lines in high-rise buildings due to its durability?
o: PPR (Polypropylene Random Copolymer) or Galvanized Iron.
questions.n: PPR is highly resistant to pressure and heat, while GI provides structural strength for vertical risers.
